Lattice point enumeration of polytopes associated to integer compositionsThanks:  Mathematics Subject Classifications: 52B20, 05A15, 05E45, 06A07Thanks:  Key words and phrases. Lattice polytope, integer composition, Ehrhart polynomial, poset, zeta polynomial, gamma-positivity.

Christos A. Athanasiadis Address: Department of Mathematics
National and Kapodistrian University of Athens
Panepistimioupolis
15784 Athens, Greece Email address: caath@math.uoa.gr
Date: November 1, 2025
Abstract.

An nn-dimensional lattice polytope 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} can be associated to any composition σ\sigma of a positive integer nn, as a special case of constructions due to Pitman–Stanley and Chapoton. The entries of the hh-vector of σ\sigma, introduced by Chapoton, enumerate the lattice points in 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} by the number of their zero coordinates. Chapoton conjectured that this vector is equal to the hh-vector of a simplicial polytope. This paper proves that the hh-vector of σ\sigma is gamma-positive, hence palindromic and unimodal, and confirms certain other conjectures of Chapoton on the lattice point enumeration of composition polytopes. A combinatorial interpretation of their h∗h^{\ast}-polynomials is deduced.

1. Introduction

A composition of a positive integer nn is defined as a sequence σ=(r1,r2,…,rk)\sigma=(r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{k}) of positive integers whose sum is equal to nn. Given such a composition σ\sigma, we consider the polytope 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} defined by the inequalities xi≥0x_{i}\geq 0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and

(1) x1+x2+⋯+xsi≤six_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}

for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, where si=r1+r2+⋯+ris_{i}=r_{1}+r_{2}+\cdots+r_{i} and x1,x2,…,xnx_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n} are the standard coordinates of ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}. We refer to the polytopes 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} in this paper as composition polytopes.

Composition polytopes are special cases of the polytopes associated to arbors (defined as rooted trees on the vertex set of blocks of a partition of a finite set), introduced and studied by Chapoton [5]. They also arise as Pitman–Stanley polytopes [12] when some of the parameters defining these polytopes are allowed to be zero. The composition polytope 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} reduces to the nnth dilate of the nn-dimensional simplex in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with vertices the origin and the unit coordinate vectors, when σ\sigma has one part, and to the Pitman–Stanley polytope with all parameters equal to 1, when all parts of σ\sigma are equal to 1.

The face lattice of composition polytopes is well understood. As observed in [12, Theorem 20], 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} is combinatorially isomorphic to a product of simplices, the dimensions of which are the parts of σ\sigma. The lattice point enumeration of composition polytopes, which is more interesting, has been studied for the more general classes of arbor polytopes [5] and Pitman–Stanley polytopes [12]. Chapoton defined the hh-vector of a composition σ\sigma of nn (more generally, of an arbor) as the sequence h⁡(σ)=(hi​(σ))0≤i≤nh(\sigma)=(h_{i}(\sigma))_{0\leq i\leq n}, where hi​(σ)h_{i}(\sigma) is the number of points in 𝒬σ∩ℕn{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma}\cap{\mathbb{N}}^{n} having exactly ii nonzero coordinates (this vector should not be confused with the hh-vector of the simple polytope 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma}). We note that h0​(σ)=hn​(σ)=1h_{0}(\sigma)=h_{n}(\sigma)=1. The following intriguing conjecture has been stated more generally for the class of arbor polytopes [5, Conjecture 0.1]; we refer to the discussion in [5, Section 0.1] for the motivation behind it.

Conjecture 1.1 ([5]).

The vector h⁡(σ)h(\sigma) is equal to the hh-vector of an nn-dimensional simplicial polytope for every composition σ\sigma of nn.

In particular, h⁡(σ)h(\sigma) should be palindromic and unimodal, meaning that hi​(σ)=hn−i​(σ)h_{i}(\sigma)=h_{n-i}(\sigma) for all 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n and h0​(σ)≤h1​(σ)≤⋯≤h⌊n/2⌋​(σ)h_{0}(\sigma)\leq h_{1}(\sigma)\leq\cdots\leq h_{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(\sigma). Moreover, it is suggested in [5, Section 0.1] that h⁡(σ)h(\sigma) should in fact be equal to the hh-vector of an nn-dimensional flag simplicial polytope. Thus, in view of Gal’s conjecture [6, Conjecture 2.1.7] (see also [1, Section 3]) on gamma-positivity, it is reasonable to expect that the generating polynomial h⁡(σ,t):=∑i=0nhi​(σ)​tih(\sigma,t):=\sum_{i=0}^{n}h_{i}(\sigma)t^{i} of h⁡(σ)h(\sigma) is γ\gamma-positive, meaning that

(2) h⁡(σ,t)=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋γi​(σ)​ti​(1+t)n−2​ih(\sigma,t)=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\gamma_{i}(\sigma)t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}

for some nonnegative integers γi​(σ)\gamma_{i}(\sigma). The first main result of this paper shows that this is indeed the case.

Theorem 1.2.

The polynomial h⁡(σ,t)h(\sigma,t) is γ\gamma-positive for every composition σ\sigma. In particular, the vector h⁡(σ)h(\sigma) is palindromic and unimodal.

Our second main result confirms another curious conjecture of Chapoton [5], concerning the Ehrhart polynomial of composition polytopes. We recall (see, for instance, [10, Section 4.6]) that the Ehrhart polynomial Ehr⁡(Q,t){\rm Ehr}(Q,t) of a lattice polytope 𝒬⊂ℝ≥0n{\mathcal{Q}}\subset{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{n} has the defining property that Ehr⁡(𝒬,m)=#⁡(m​𝒬∩ℕn){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},m)=\#(m{\mathcal{Q}}\cap{\mathbb{N}}^{n}) for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. The zeta polynomial (see [10, Section 3.12]) 𝒵⁡(P,t){\mathcal{Z}}(P,t) of a finite poset (P,⪯)(P,\preceq) has the defining property that 𝒵⁡(P,m+1){\mathcal{Z}}(P,m+1) is equal to the number of mm-element multichains in PP, meaning sequences (p1,p2,…,pm)(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{m}) of elements of PP such that p1⪯p2⪯⋯⪯pmp_{1}\preceq p_{2}\preceq\cdots\preceq p_{m}, for every m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}. Given a composition σ\sigma of nn, Chapoton [5, Section 1] has considered the set PσP_{\sigma} of lattice points in 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} as a subposet of the product poset ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Theorem 1.3.

([5, Conjecture 3.1]) We have Ehr⁡(𝒬σ,t)=𝒵⁡(Prev⁡(σ),t+1){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma},t)={\mathcal{Z}}(P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)},t+1) for every composition σ\sigma, where rev⁡(σ){\rm rev}(\sigma) is the composition obtained from σ\sigma by reversing the order in which the parts of σ\sigma appear.

Here is another intriguing conjecture from [5], stated there for all arbor polytopes (see [5, Conjecture 2.2]), on which no progress is made in this paper.

Conjecture 1.4 ([5]).

For every composition σ\sigma, all roots of the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} are real and lie in the interval [−1,0][-1,0].

Theorem 1.2 is proven in Section 2; the proof yields an explicit combinatorial interpretation of the numbers γi​(σ)\gamma_{i}(\sigma) which appear in Equation (2) (see Proposition 2.2). Section 2 also shows that h⁡(σ)=h⁡(rev⁡(σ))h(\sigma)=h({\rm rev}(\sigma)) for every composition σ\sigma. Two proofs of Theorem 1.3, one essentially bijective and another based on the results of [12, Section 3], are given in Section 3 and a combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} is deduced via the theory of pure shellability of posets (see Proposition 3.2). While this paper is restricted to composition polytopes, we do hope that some of the arguments presented here can be extended to more general classes of lattice polytopes.

Throughout this paper, we set ℕ={0,1,2,…}{\mathbb{N}}=\{0,1,2,\dots\} and [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\} for n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. We denote by #​S\#S the cardinality of a finite set SS and write σ⊧n\sigma\models n when σ\sigma is a composition of nn. Our notation and terminology about posets follows [10, Chapter 3]. Background on Ehrhart theory and face enumeration of simplicial complexes and polytopes can be found in [3, 7] [10, Chapter 4] and [9], respectively.

2. Gamma-positivity

This section proves Theorem 1.2 and shows (see Proposition 2.5) that h⁡(σ)=h⁡(rev⁡(σ))h(\sigma)=h({\rm rev}(\sigma)) for every composition σ\sigma.

Throughout this section we let σ=(r1,r2,…,rk)\sigma=(r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{k}) be a composition of nn and set si=r1+r2+⋯+ris_{i}=r_{1}+r_{2}+\cdots+r_{i} for i∈[k]i\in[k]. We recall that PσP_{\sigma} consists of all points (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that

a1+a2+⋯+asi≤sia_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}

for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. We record such a point by the nn-tuple (p1,p2,…,pn)∈ℕn(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, where

pi={a1+a2+⋯+ai,if ai≥10,if ai=0p_{i}=\begin{cases}a_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{i},&\text{if $a_{i}\geq 1$}\\ 0,&\text{if $a_{i}=0$}\\ \end{cases}

for every i∈[n]i\in[n]. As a running example, if σ=(3,4,2)\sigma=(3,4,2), then (0,0,2,0,4,0,0,3,0)∈Pσ(0,0,2,0,4,0,0,3,0)\in P_{\sigma} is recorded by the tuple (0,0,2,0,6,0,0,9,0)(0,0,2,0,6,0,0,9,0). The map just described shows that PσP_{\sigma} is in one-to-one correspondence with the set, say ℋσ{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}, of nn-tuples (p1,p2,…,pn)∈ℕn(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} consisting of positive integers which appear in strictly increasing order from left to right and zeros, such that p1,p2,…,psi≤sip_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i} for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. Moreover, hj​(σ)h_{j}(\sigma) is equal to the number of elements of ℋσ{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} which have exactly jj nonzero entries.

Given x∈ℋσx\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}, we denote by S⁡(x)S(x) the set of positions of the nonzero entries in xx and by T⁡(x)T(x) the set of these entries. Thus, in our running example, we have S⁡(x)={3,5,8}S(x)=\{3,5,8\} and T⁡(x)={2,6,9}T(x)=\{2,6,9\}. Clearly, S⁡(x),T⁡(x)⊆[n]S(x),T(x)\subseteq[n] and #​S​(x)=#​T​(x)\#S(x)=\#T(x) for every x∈ℋσx\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}. Moreover, every x∈ℋσx\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} is determined by S⁡(x)S(x) and T⁡(x)T(x) and

(3) h⁡(σ,t)=∑x∈ℋσt#​S​(x).h(\sigma,t)=\sum_{x\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma}}t^{\#S(x)}.
Lemma 2.1.

Let S,TS,T be subsets of [n][n] of equal cardinalities and let R⊆[n]R\subseteq[n] be disjoint from S∪TS\cup T. Then, the pair (S,T)(S,T) has the property that S=S⁡(x)S=S(x) and T=T⁡(x)T=T(x) for some x∈ℋσx\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} if and only if so does (S∪R,T∪R)(S\cup R,T\cup R).

Proof.

We may assume that RR has a single element r∈[n]r\in[n]. Let x=(p1,p2,…,pn)∈ℕnx=(p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} be the nn-tuple which has the elements of TT as its nonzero entries and these appear in strictly increasing order from left to right in the positions of the elements of SS. Similarly, let y=(q1,q2,…,qn)∈ℕny=(q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} be the nn-tuple which has the elements of T∪{r}T\cup\{r\} as its nonzero entries and these appear in strictly increasing order from left to right in the positions of the elements of S∪{r}S\cup\{r\}. We have x∈ℋσx\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} if and only if

(4) p1,p2,…,psi≤sifor every​i∈[k]p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}\ \ \text{for every}\ i\in[k]

and y∈ℋσy\in{\mathcal{H}}_{\sigma} if and only if

(5) q1,q2,…,qsi≤sifor every​i∈[k].q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}\ \ \text{for every}\ i\in[k].

Thus, we have to show the equivalence of (4) and (5). This is obvious if qr=rq_{r}=r, since then xx and yy differ only in the rrth coordinate. Suppose that r=qsr=q_{s} for some s>rs>r. Then, yy is obtained from xx by placing rr in position ss and shifting to the left some nonzero entries, all less than rr, within positions r,r+1,…,sr,r+1,\dots,s. Finally, if r=qsr=q_{s} for some s<rs<r, then yy is obtained from xx by placing rr in position ss and shifting to the right some nonzero entries, all larger than rr, within positions s,s+1,…,rs,s+1,\dots,r. The equivalence (4) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (5) holds in either case. ∎

T⁡(x)∖(S⁡(x)∩T⁡(x))\displaystyle T(x){\smallsetminus}(S(x)\cap T(x)) =T⁡(y)∖(S⁡(y)∩T⁡(y)).\displaystyle=T(y){\smallsetminus}(S(y)\cap T(y)).

As a result,

∑y∈Cxt#​S​(y)=∑R⊆[n]∖(S⁡(x)∪T⁡(x))t#⁡(S⁡(x)∪R)=t#​S​(x)​(1+t)n−2​#​S​(x).\sum_{y\in C_{x}}t^{\#S(y)}=\sum_{R\subseteq[n]{\smallsetminus}(S(x)\cup T(x))}t^{\#(S(x)\cup R)}=t^{\#S(x)}(1+t)^{n-2\,\#S(x)}.

Example 2.3.

Let σ=(n)\sigma=(n) be the composition of nn with only one part. Then, PσP_{\sigma} consists of all points (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that a1+a2+⋯+an≤na_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\leq n, hi​(σ)h_{i}(\sigma) is equal to the total number of pairs (S,T)(S,T) of ii-element subsets of [n][n] and γi​(σ)\gamma_{i}(\sigma) is equal to the number of such pairs (S,T)(S,T) with S∩T=∅S\cap T=\varnothing. Hence, hi​(σ)=(ni)2h_{i}(\sigma)={n\choose i}^{2} for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n and γi​(σ)=(ni)​(n−ii)\gamma_{i}(\sigma)={n\choose i}{n-i\choose i} for 0≤i≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq i\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor and Proposition 2.2 specializes to the well known identity

∑i=0n(ni)2​ti=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋(ni)​(n−ii)​ti​(1+t)n−2​i\sum_{i=0}^{n}{n\choose i}^{2}t^{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}{n\choose i}{n-i\choose i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}

(see [1, Theorem 2.32] for a generalization in the setting of finite Coxeter groups). ∎

For the remainder of this section we represent elements of ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with sum of coordinates at most nn by lattice paths in the x​yxy-plane as follows. A point (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with a1+a2+⋯+an≤na_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\leq n is represented by the lattice path with initial vertex (−1,0)(-1,0), terminal vertex (n,n+1)(n,n+1) and east (E) or north (N) unit steps, so that the initial and final steps are east and north, respectively, and the height of the part of the lattice path within the strip j−1≤x≤jj-1\leq x\leq j is a1+a2+⋯+aja_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{j} for every j∈[n]j\in[n]. We observe that the number of nonzero entries of such an element of ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} is equal to one less than the number of east-north corners of the associated lattice path.

We denote by 𝒢n{\mathcal{G}}_{n} the set of lattice paths which represent the elements of ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with sum of coordinates at most nn and let Γσ∈𝒢n\Gamma_{\sigma}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{n} be the lattice path associated to the nn-tuple with entry sis_{i} in position si−1+1s_{i-1}+1 for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k (where s0:=0s_{0}:=0) and all other entries equal to zero. Thus, Γσ\Gamma_{\sigma} has successive steps east, followed by r1r_{1} north and r1r_{1} east steps, followed by r2r_{2} north and r2r_{2} east steps, and so on, followed by a string of north steps at the end. Then, the elements of PσP_{\sigma} are represented by the lattice paths in 𝒢n{\mathcal{G}}_{n} which lie weakly below Γσ\Gamma_{\sigma}.

Example 2.4.

Let σ=(1,1,…,1)⊧n\sigma=(1,1,\dots,1)\models n, so that PσP_{\sigma} consists of all points (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that a1+a2+⋯+aj≤ja_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{j}\leq j for every j∈[n]j\in[n]. The lattice path Γσ\Gamma_{\sigma} has successive steps ENEN⋯EN\textrm{ENEN}\cdots\textrm{EN} and the total number of lattice paths in 𝒢n{\mathcal{G}}_{n} which lie weakly below it (and hence the cardinality of PσP_{\sigma}) is well known to equal the Catalan number 1n+2​(2​n+2n+1)\frac{1}{n+2}{2n+2\choose n+1}. Moreover, counting these lattice paths by the number of east-north corners shows that hi​(σ)h_{i}(\sigma) is equal to the Narayana number

hi​(σ)=1i+1​(ni)​(n+1i)h_{i}(\sigma)=\frac{1}{i+1}{n\choose i}{n+1\choose i}

for 0≤i≤n0\leq i\leq n (see, for instance, [11, Problem A.46]).

By Proposition 2.2, γi​(σ)\gamma_{i}(\sigma) is equal to the number of pairs (S,T)(S,T) of disjoint ii-element subsets of [n][n] such that the rrth largest element of TT is smaller that the rrth largest element of SS for every rr. Since these pairs are in one-to-one correspondence with Young tableaux of shape (i,i)(i,i) with entries in [n][n], we have

γi​(σ)\displaystyle\gamma_{i}(\sigma) =(n2​i)⋅1i+1​(2​ii)=1i+1⋅n!(i!)2​(n−2​i)!\displaystyle={n\choose 2i}\cdot\frac{1}{i+1}{2i\choose i}=\frac{1}{i+1}\cdot\frac{n!}{(i!)^{2}\,(n-2i)!}
=1i+1​(ni)​(n−ii)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{i+1}{n\choose i}{n-i\choose i}

for 0≤i≤⌊n/2⌋0\leq i\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor and Proposition 2.2 specializes to the well known identity

∑i=0n1i+1​(ni)​(n+1i)​ti=∑i=0⌊n/2⌋1i+1​(ni)​(n−ii)​ti​(1+t)n−2​i\sum_{i=0}^{n}\frac{1}{i+1}{n\choose i}{n+1\choose i}t^{i}=\sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{1}{i+1}{n\choose i}{n-i\choose i}t^{i}(1+t)^{n-2i}

(see, for instance, again [1, Theorem 2.32]). ∎

We conclude this section with the following statement.

Proposition 2.5.

([5, Conjecture 3.2]) We have h⁡(σ)=h⁡(rev⁡(σ))h(\sigma)=h({\rm rev}(\sigma)) for every σ⊧n\sigma\models n.

Proof.

We observe that orthogonal reflection in the line x+y=nx+y=n maps Γσ\Gamma_{\sigma} to Γrev⁡(σ)\Gamma_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)} and hence induces a bijection from the set of lattice paths which represent the elements of PσP_{\sigma} to the set of those for Prev⁡(σ)P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)}. We also observe that the number of east-north corners of a lattice path is preserved under this bijection and the proof follows. ∎

3. Ehrhart and Zeta polynomials

This section offers two proofs of Theorem 1.2 and deduces a combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of the composition polytope 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma}. As in the previous section, σ=(r1,r2,…,rk)\sigma=(r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{k}) is a composition of nn and si=r1+r2+⋯+ris_{i}=r_{1}+r_{2}+\cdots+r_{i} for 0≤i≤k0\leq i\leq k, where s0:=0s_{0}:=0.

We recall that ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} is partially ordered as a direct product, meaning that for x,y∈ℕnx,y\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with x=(a1,a2,…,an)x=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) and y=(b1,b2,…,bn)y=(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n}) we have x⪯yx\preceq y if and only if ai≤bia_{i}\leq b_{i} for every i∈[n]i\in[n], where ⪯\preceq stands for the partial order of ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n}.

Lemma 3.1.

There is a one-to-one correspondence from the set of mm-multichains in ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with a given maximal element (a1,a2,…,an)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) to the set of solutions (bi,j)1≤i≤n, 1≤j≤m∈ℕm​n(b_{i,j})_{1\leq i\leq n,\,1\leq j\leq m}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{mn} of the system of linear equations

xi,1+xi,2+⋯+xi,m=aix_{i,1}+x_{i,2}+\cdots+x_{i,m}=a_{i}

for i∈[n]i\in[n].

Proof.

By definition of the product order ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, it suffices to verify the statement for n=1n=1, which is a trivial task. ∎

First proof of Theorem 1.3.

For any m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}}, Ehr⁡(Qσ,m){\rm Ehr}(Q_{\sigma},m) is equal to the number of points (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that

(6) a1+a2+⋯+asi≤si​ma_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}m

for i∈[k]i\in[k]. Thus, for i=ki=k we get a1+a2+⋯+an≤m​na_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{n}\leq mn. Let’s consider the partial sums a1+a2+⋯+aia_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{i} and, for 0≤j≤m​n0\leq j\leq mn, let’s denote by bjb_{j} the number of indices i∈[n]i\in[n] for which a1+a2+⋯+ai=ja_{1}+a_{2}+\cdots+a_{i}=j (the reader may want to interpret the bjb_{j} when (a1,a2,…,an)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) is represented by a lattice path, as in Section 2). Then,

(7) b0+b1+⋯+bm​n=nb_{0}+b_{1}+\cdots+b_{mn}=n

and

(8) b0+b1+⋯+bsi​m≥sib_{0}+b_{1}+\cdots+b_{s_{i}m}\geq s_{i}

for i∈[k]i\in[k]. Moreover, the map which sends (a1,a2,…,an)(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}) to (b0,b1,…,bm​n)(b_{0},b_{1},\dots,b_{mn}) is a one-to-one correspondence from the set of solutions (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} of the system of linear inequalities (6) to the set of solutions (b0,b1,…,bm​n)∈ℕm​n+1(b_{0},b_{1},\dots,b_{mn})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{mn+1} of the system of linear equalities and inequalities (7) and (8). Eliminating b0b_{0} we find that the latter set is in one-to-one correspondence with the set of solutions (b1,b2,…,bm​n)∈ℕm​n(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{mn})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{mn} of the system of linear inequalities

(9) bsi​m+1+bsi​m+2+⋯+bm​n≤n−sib_{s_{i}m+1}+b_{s_{i}m+2}+\cdots+b_{mn}\leq n-s_{i}

for i∈[k−1]i\in[k-1] and

(10) b1+b2+⋯+bm​n≤n.b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{mn}\leq n.

The number of these solutions is equal to the number 𝒵⁡(Prev⁡(σ),m+1){\mathcal{Z}}(P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)},m+1) of mm-multichains in Prev⁡(σ)P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)}. This follows from the fact that, since n−si=ri+1+ri+2+⋯+rkn-s_{i}=r_{i+1}+r_{i+2}+\cdots+r_{k}, the set Prev⁡(σ)P_{{\rm rev}(\sigma)} consists of all tuples (x1,x2,…,xn)∈ℕn(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that

xsi+1+xsi+2+⋯+xn≤n−six_{s_{i}+1}+x_{s_{i}+2}+\cdots+x_{n}\leq n-s_{i}

for 0≤i<k0\leq i<k and from Lemma 3.1. ∎

Part of our second proof of Theorem 1.3 follows the proof of [12, Equation (33)], which is a formula for the number of lattice points of a Pitman–Stanley polytope. To avoid making too long of a digression, we assume familiarity with Sections 3 and 4 of [12] and only sketch this part of the proof.

Second proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let us consider the poset Ωσ\Omega_{\sigma} which consists of two disjoint chains α1≺α2≺⋯≺αn\alpha_{1}\prec\alpha_{2}\prec\cdots\prec\alpha_{n} and β1≺β2≺⋯≺βn\beta_{1}\prec\beta_{2}\prec\cdots\prec\beta_{n}, together with the additional cover relations αsi≺βsi\alpha_{s_{i}}\prec\beta_{s_{i}} for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. We let C={β1,β2,…,βn}C=\{\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\dots,\beta_{n}\} and 𝐮=(u1,u2,…,un){\mathbf{u}}=(u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{n}), where uj=j​mu_{j}=jm for every j∈[n]j\in[n] and where m∈ℕm\in{\mathbb{N}} is fixed. In this situation, Pitman and Stanley [12, Section 3] have defined the order cone section 𝒞C​(Ωσ,𝐮){\mathcal{C}}_{C}(\Omega_{\sigma},{\mathbf{u}}) as the polytope of all order preserving maps f:Ωσ→ℝ≥0f:\Omega_{\sigma}\rightarrow{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0} such that f⁡(βj)=ujf(\beta_{j})=u_{j} for every j∈[n]j\in[n]. Setting fj=f⁡(αj)f_{j}=f(\alpha_{j}) for every j∈[n]j\in[n] and f0=0f_{0}=0 we have

0=f0≤f1≤⋯≤fn0=f_{0}\leq f_{1}\leq\cdots\leq f_{n}

and

fsi≤si​mf_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i}m

for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. The transformation xj=fj−fj−1x_{j}=f_{j}-f_{j-1} for j∈[n]j\in[n] then shows that 𝒞C​(Ωσ,𝐮){\mathcal{C}}_{C}(\Omega_{\sigma},{\mathbf{u}}) is integrally equivalent to m​𝒬σm{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma}. Theorem 5 in [12] expresses the number of lattice points of 𝒞C​(Ωσ,𝐮){\mathcal{C}}_{C}(\Omega_{\sigma},{\mathbf{u}}) as a sum over all linear extensions of Ωσ\Omega_{\sigma}. Such a linear extension is uniquely determined by the positions, say 1≤j1<j2<⋯<jn≤2​n1\leq j_{1}<j_{2}<\cdots<j_{n}\leq 2n, of β1,β2,…,βn\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\dots,\beta_{n}, which must satisfy jsi≥2​sij_{s_{i}}\geq 2s_{i} for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. Thus, setting κi=ji−ji−1−1\kappa_{i}=j_{i}-j_{i-1}-1 for i∈[n]i\in[n] (where j0=0j_{0}=0), the argument of [12, p. 617] shows that in our situation, [12, Theorem 5] yields the formula

λsi+1+λsi+2+⋯+λn≤n−si\lambda_{s_{i}+1}+\lambda_{s_{i}+2}+\cdots+\lambda_{n}\leq n-s_{i}

We now present the final main result of this paper. We recall that the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial of an nn-dimensional polytope in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with vertices in ℤn{\mathbb{Z}}^{n} is defined by the equation

(12) ∑m≥0Ehr⁡(𝒬,m)​tm=h∗​(𝒬,t)(1−x)n+1.\sum_{m\geq 0}{\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}},m)t^{m}=\frac{h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}},t)}{(1-x)^{n+1}}.

Given a word w=(w1,w2,…,wn)∈[n]nw=(w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{n})\in[n]^{n}, we denote by asc⁡(w){\rm asc}(w) the number of indices (called ascents) i∈[n]i\in[n] such that wi−1<wiw_{i-1}<w_{i}, where w0:=1w_{0}:=1.

Proposition 3.2.

We have

(13) h∗​(𝒬σ,t)=∑wtasc⁡(w),h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma},t)=\sum_{w}t^{{\rm asc}(w)},

where ww ranges over all words w∈[n]nw\in[n]^{n} which have at least sis_{i} entries less than or equal to sis_{i} for every i∈[k]i\in[k]. Equivalently, the unique nondecreasing rearrangement (u1,u2,…,un)(u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{n}) of ww should satisfy usi≤siu_{s_{i}}\leq s_{i} for every i∈[k]i\in[k].

The proof employs the basics of the theory of EL-shellability of posets [4] [13, Lecture 3], which we briefly recall. Let (P,⪯)(P,\preceq) be a finite graded poset which has a minimum element 0^\hat{0} and a maximum element 1^\hat{1} and let ℰ⁡(P){\mathcal{E}}(P) be the set of covering relations of PP. An edge labeling of PP (with integer labels) is any map λ:ℰ⁡(P)→ℤ\lambda:{\mathcal{E}}(P)\rightarrow{\mathbb{Z}}. Let CC be an unrefinable chain p0≺p1≺⋯≺pmp_{0}\prec p_{1}\prec\cdots\prec p_{m} of elements of PP, so that (pi−1,pi)∈ℰ⁡(P)(p_{i-1},p_{i})\in{\mathcal{E}}(P) for every i∈[m]i\in[m]. We define the label of CC with respect to λ\lambda as the sequence

λ⁡(C)=(λ⁡(p0,p1),λ⁡(p1,p2),…,λ⁡(pm−1,pm))\lambda(C)=(\lambda(p_{0},p_{1}),\lambda(p_{1},p_{2}),\dots,\lambda(p_{m-1},p_{m}))

and the descent set of CC as Des⁡(C)={i∈[m−1]:λ⁡(pi−1,pi)>λ⁡(pi,pi+1)}{\rm Des}(C)=\{i\in[m-1]:\lambda(p_{i-1},p_{i})>\lambda(p_{i},p_{i+1})\}. We say that CC is rising with respect to λ\lambda if λ⁡(C)\lambda(C) is weakly increasing and that CC is lexicographically smaller (with respect to λ\lambda) than an unrefinable chain C′C^{\prime} in PP of the same length if λ⁡(C)\lambda(C) precedes λ⁡(C′)\lambda(C^{\prime}) in the lexicographic order. An edge labeling λ\lambda of PP is called an EL-labeling if for every nonsingleton interval [u,v][u,v] in PP: (i) there is a unique rising (with respect to λ\lambda) maximal chain in [u,v][u,v]; and (ii) this chain is lexicographically smallest among all maximal chains in [u,v][u,v]. Then

(14) h⁡(Δ⁡(P),t)=∑C∈ℳ⁡(P)tdes⁡(C),h(\Delta(P),t)=\sum_{C\in{\mathcal{M}}(P)}t^{{\rm des}(C)},

where ℳ⁡(P){\mathcal{M}}(P) is the set of all maximal chains of PP and des⁡(C)=#​Des​(C){\rm des}(C)=\#{\rm Des}(C) is the number of descents of CC for C∈ℳ⁡(P)C\in{\mathcal{M}}(P). Here Δ⁡(P)\Delta(P) stands for the order complex of PP (meaning, the simplicial complex consisting of all chains in PP) and the hh-polynomial of Δ⁡(P)\Delta(P) is defined as h⁡(Δ⁡(P),t)=∑F∈Δ⁡(P)t#​F​(1−t)d+1−(#​F)h(\Delta(P),t)=\sum_{F\in\Delta(P)}t^{\#F}(1-t)^{d+1-(\#F)}, where dd is the rank of PP.

Proof of Proposition 3.2.

Let us write τ=rev⁡(σ)\tau={\rm rev}(\sigma). By Equation (12) applied to 𝒬σ{\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma} and since

∑m≥0𝒵⁡(Pτ,m+1)​tm=h⁡(Δ⁡(Pτ),t)(1−t)n+1\sum_{m\geq 0}{\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},m+1)t^{m}=\frac{h(\Delta(P_{\tau}),t)}{(1-t)^{n+1}}

(see, for instance, [2, Equation (8)]) and Ehr⁡(𝒬σ,t)=𝒵⁡(Pτ,t+1){\rm Ehr}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma},t)={\mathcal{Z}}(P_{\tau},t+1) by Theorem 1.3, we have h∗​(𝒬σ,t)=h⁡(Δ⁡(Pτ),t)h^{\ast}({\mathcal{Q}}_{\sigma},t)=h(\Delta(P_{\tau}),t). Thus, it suffices to show that h⁡(Δ⁡(Pτ),t)h(\Delta(P_{\tau}),t) is equal to the sum on the right-hand side of Equation (13).

For that reason, we consider the following edge labeling of the poset P^τ=Pτ∪{1^}\widehat{P}_{\tau}=P_{\tau}\cup\{\hat{1}\}, obtained from PτP_{\tau} by adding a maximum element 1^\hat{1}. We recall that PτP_{\tau} is the subposet of the product order ℕn{\mathbb{N}}^{n} consisting of all points (a1,a2,…,an)∈ℕn(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} such that

asi+1+asi+2+⋯+an≤ri+1+ri+2+⋯+rk=n−sia_{s_{i}+1}+a_{s_{i}+2}+\cdots+a_{n}\leq r_{i+1}+r_{i+2}+\cdots+r_{k}=n-s_{i}

for 0≤i<n0\leq i<n. The cover relations are the pairs (u,v)∈Pτ×Pτ(u,v)\in P_{\tau}\times P_{\tau} such that vv can be obtained from uu by adding 1 in one of its coordinates. Given such a pair we set λ⁡(u,v)=i\lambda(u,v)=i, if uu and vv differ in the iith coordinate. We also set λ⁡(u,1^)=1\lambda(u,\hat{1})=1 for every maximal element u∈Pτu\in P_{\tau} and claim that the resulting edge labeling λ:ℰ⁡(P^τ)→ℤ\lambda:{\mathcal{E}}(\widehat{P}_{\tau})\rightarrow{\mathbb{Z}} is an EL-labeling. Given a nonsingleton closed interval [u,v][u,v] of P^τ\widehat{P}_{\tau}, we need to verify that there is a unique rising (with respect to λ\lambda) maximal chain in [u,v][u,v] and that this chain is lexicographically least among all maximal chains of [u,v][u,v]. This holds in case v≠1^v\neq\hat{1} because then the labels of the maximal chains of [u,v][u,v] are exactly the permutations of a multiset; it holds if v=1^v=\hat{1} as well since then there is a unique maximal chain with label (1,1,…,1)(1,1,\dots,1) and this chain is the only rising maximal chain of [u,v][u,v].

Since λ\lambda is an EL-labeling, by Equation (14) we have

h⁡(Δ⁡(Pτ),t)=∑wtdes⁡(w),h(\Delta(P_{\tau}),t)=\sum_{w}t^{{\rm des}(w)},

where w=(wn,…,w1,w0)w=(w_{n},\dots,w_{1},w_{0}) ranges over the labels of all maximal chains of P^τ\widehat{P}_{\tau} and des⁡(w){\rm des}(w) is the number of indices i∈[n]i\in[n] such that wi>wi−1w_{i}>w_{i-1}. We observe that ww is such a label if and only if w0=1w_{0}=1 and at least sis_{i} entries of (wn,…,w2,w1)(w_{n},\dots,w_{2},w_{1}) are less than or equal to sis_{i} for every i∈[k]i\in[k] and the proof follows. ∎

Remark 3.3.

Proposition 3.2 specializes to a well known combinatorial interpretation of the h∗h^{\ast}-polynomial (equivalently, of the hh-polynomial of the nn-fold edgewise subdivision) of the standard nn-dimensional simplex when σ=(n)\sigma=(n) has one part; see, for instance, [8, Corollary 8] for a generalization and refinement. A generalization of Proposition 3.2, valid for the polytopes in ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} defined by the equations

x1+x2+⋯+xsi≤c1+c2+⋯+cix_{1}+x_{2}+\cdots+x_{s_{i}}\leq c_{1}+c_{2}+\cdots+c_{i}

for 1≤i≤k1\leq i\leq k, where c1,c2,…,ckc_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{k} are positive integers, has been found by Xue Yan [14].
